newsitem.title: USA: Cardinal led Chicago archdiocese for 14 years.
newsitem.headline: Cardinal led Chicago archdiocese for 14 years.

text.p: Cardinal Joseph Bernardin, who died early on Thursday after battling pancreatic cancer for more than a year, built a prayerful, saintly image in 14 years as Chicago's cardinal-archbishop, a presence that touched his flock all the more in his final months.

The spare and soft-spoken son of an Italian stone cutter, the 68-year-old Bernardin was the longest-serving active U.S. cardinal, appointed by Pope John Paul II in 1982 to head the 2.3 million member Chicago archdiocese, the nation's second-largest after Los Angeles.

He was a moderate voice among liberals and conservatives in the ranks of the bishops, and in August launched a series of dialogues designed to heal rifts that he said threatened to pull the church apart.

During his tenure, Bernardin became deeply involved in world church issues, playing a prominent role in drafting U.S. church policy addressing war, peace and nuclear arms, and for seven years headed the bishops' anti-abortion policy committee, espousing a policy describing human life in all its forms as a "seamless garment" which cannot be rent.

In one of his last public acts, Bernardin proclaimed his firm opposition to physician-assisted suicide in a letter directed to the Supreme Court as it prepared to decide a number of cases on the issue.

In June 1995, Bernardin was found to be suffering from pancreatic cancer, a particularly deadly form of the disease, and underwent surgery. He resumed his duties while undergoing painful chemotherapy treatments, but in a dramatic news conference held on Aug. 30, he announced the disease had spread to his liver and was inoperable, giving him less than a year to live.

He promised to "serve until the end," and in a moving statement about his imminent death he said: "I consider this as God's special gift to me at this particular moment in my life. As a person of faith, I see death as a friend, as the transition from earthly life to life eternal."
In his frequent hospital visits, Bernardin often counselled other patients and said he became more aware of his own vulnerabilities. "I can say in all sincerity that I am at peace," he said.

In 1993, Bernardin was hit by a $10 million suit alleging that he sexually abused a teenaged boy in the 1970s while both were at an Ohio seminary. But the former student later recanted the charges against Bernardin, saying his memories were flawed, and the two later prayed together.

Bernardin, born in Columbia, South Carolina, began his career in his native state where he spent 14 years in the diocese of Charleston. In 1972 he became archbishop of Cincinnati before moving on to Chicago.
He was popular among his fellow priests in the archdiocese, where he encouraged collegiality.
